metaDescription: Five electric tankless water heaters at or under $500, from a Rheem 18kW 240V and ThermoMate 6kW to 4500W and 3.5kW point-of-use units, with real flow numbers.
expertTake: The Rheem 18 kW 240V heater is the pick at this cap because it is the only unit here with enough power for more than a trickle, up to 4.4 gallons per minute in warm inlet water. The ThermoMate 6 kW is the value choice for a single sink or a laundry tub with ETL listing. Anyone with a standard residential panel should price the electrical work first, since 18 kW needs heavy wiring.
introParagraphs: Raising the budget past the small point-of-use class buys real power. The jump from a few kilowatts to double digits is the difference between warming a handwashing stream and delivering a respectable flow, and it is also the difference between a simple plug-in project and a serious electrical job.

Prices move, and the $500 cap used here reflects live listing prices when this guide was updated. The lineup spans one very powerful unit and several smaller ones, so the guide spends its effort on the arithmetic that decides whether any of them can work in a given house: flow, temperature rise, amperage and panel capacity.

products.name: Rheem 18 kW 240V Tankless Electric Water Heater with Digital Thermostat

specList.label: Control
specList.value: External digital thermostat, plus or minus 1 degree

products.description:
The Rheem 18 kW is a 240 volt unit with an external digital thermostat accurate to one degree, two copper immersion heating elements that can be serviced in the field and a flow rating of up to 4.4 gallons per minute. Self-modulating power adjusts the load to meet demand, so the heater does not draw full power for a trickle. It is the only unit in this guide with enough power to supply more than one small fixture.

The 4.4 gallon figure is a best case at a small temperature rise, and the arithmetic is worth doing: an 18 kW element lifts about 123 divided by the rise in degrees Fahrenheit gallons per minute, so a 70 degree rise gives roughly 1.75 GPM. That is enough for a bathroom sink and a low-flow shower head in warm climates but not for a cold-inlet whole house. Against the ThermoMate 6 kW, it has three times the power and three times the electrical demand.

The load is about 75 amps at 240 volts, which means heavy wire, large breakers and often a panel upgrade, so the electrical work can cost as much as the heater. Descale the elements on schedule and clean the inlet screen. Replacement elements are serviceable, which is a real advantage over sealed cheap units. In a warm region where incoming water sits near 70 degrees, a low-flow shower head at about 1.5 GPM is realistic, and the unit modulates power down when you turn the valve back. For a cold region, plan on using it for a bathroom sink and nothing larger, and keep your main heater for showers.
products.bestFor: Homes with a robust electrical panel that need real flow at one or two fixtures.
pros: Up to 4.4 GPM in warm inlet water
cons: Flow drops sharply in cold inlet water

products.name: ThermoMate 6 kW 240V Hardwired Tankless Water Heater, ETL Listed

specList.label: Element
specList.value: Cast aluminum, separated from the water line

products.description:
The ThermoMate 6 kW is a 240 volt, hardwired point-of-use heater with an ETL listing that provides 1.0 gallon per minute at a 35 degree Fahrenheit temperature rise. A cast aluminum heating element separated from the water line aims to reduce scale and corrosion, and the listing quotes 99.8 percent efficiency, which is typical of resistance heating. The flow and rise are both stated, which makes it easy to judge.

The 35 degree rise is the key number, since it tells you the water will be warmed from, say, 70 to 105 degrees at 1.0 GPM, which is comfortable for hand washing in a warm climate but less so in a cold basement. Next to the 4500W units, it has about a third more power and an ETL listing. Set beside the Rheem 18 kW, it draws about 25 amps instead of 75, which is a much easier electrical job.

Have a licensed electrician hardwire it on a dedicated breaker. Descale and clean the inlet screen yearly. Mount it near the fixture to shorten the cold-water wait. A laundry tub fills slowly, and 1.0 GPM at a 35 degree rise is plenty for rinsing and soaking, which is the sort of low-demand job this size does well. Mark the breaker as dedicated at the panel, so nobody adds another load to that circuit later.
products.bestFor: A laundry tub, workshop sink or bathroom sink where a listed 240V unit makes sense.
cons: 35F rise is modest in cold climates

products.name: 4500W Electric Tankless Under-Sink Water Heater with IPX4 and Touch Control

specList.label: Use
specList.value: Point of use under a sink

products.description:
This 4500 watt under-sink heater lists IPX4 waterproofing, smart touch temperature control and a wall-mounted, space-saving design. The IPX4 rating means the housing resists splashing, which is useful under a sink. It is a point-of-use unit for a single fixture.

The listing does not give a flow rate or an ETL listing, so you must infer from the 4500 watts: it will lift about 0.5 to 0.8 gallons per minute by 70 degrees. Measured against the ThermoMate 6 kW, it has less power and less documentation. Against the Rheem 3.5 kW, it has more power but no maker with a long record.

Confirm the supply voltage and current requirement before ordering, and have an electrician install it. Keep the unit above any potential water level, since IPX4 does not cover flooding. Clean the inlet screen yearly. Because the listing does not give an amp draw, ask the seller for it or read the nameplate before the electrician sizes the breaker, since guessing is how overloaded circuits happen.
products.bestFor: Single sinks where touch control and splash protection are wanted.

products.name: Rheem 3.5 kW Point-of-Use Thermostatic Tankless Electric Water Heater, 120V

specList.label: Use
specList.value: One fixture, such as a basement sink

products.description:
The Rheem 3.5 kW appears again as the small, established option, a 120 volt thermostatic unit that supplies up to 0.5 gallons per minute for one fixture. The listing tells the buyer to verify electrical requirements, which is the right advice. It is built for a basement sink or a garage workshop.

At this cap, it is the lowest-power choice and the simplest conceptually. Next to the 6 kW ThermoMate, it has about half the power and half the flow but a more familiar brand. Set beside the 18 kW Rheem, it is a tiny unit suited to hand washing only.

A dedicated 30 amp circuit is still required, so the electrical job is not trivial. Clean the inlet screen and descale as needed. Do not expect it to run two taps. If you find that you often need a bit more heat than it gives, close the tap down slightly, which raises the outlet temperature at the cost of flow. Pair it with a faucet aerator rated for low flow so the stream still feels full at a half gallon per minute.
products.bestFor: A single basement or workshop sink with a trusted brand.
pros: Lower power for a simple job

products.name: ThermoMate 3500W 120V Tankless Electric Water Heater, 29.2 Amp, Hardwired

specList.label: Element
specList.value: Cast aluminum, separated from the water line

products.description:
The ThermoMate 3500W lists 29.2 amps of draw, 0.4 to 0.66 gallons per minute and a hardwired install. It automatically adjusts power with inlet flow and temperature. The cast aluminum element is separate from the water line.

It is the best documented 120 volt unit, because the amps and the flow range are both stated. Measured against the 6 kW ThermoMate, it is smaller and uses the common 120 volt supply, though it still demands a dedicated circuit. Against the Rheem 3.5 kW, it adds the flow range and a longer spec list.

Have an electrician hardwire it on a dedicated 30 amp breaker. Descale and clean the screen. Treat it as a handwashing unit. Because it modulates power with flow and inlet temperature, the water temperature stays steadier than on a plain on-off element when pressure changes. Even so, a toilet flush elsewhere in the house can briefly change the flow, so expect small swings.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a 120V option with stated amps and flow.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The flow a tankless heater delivers equals its power in BTU per hour divided by 500 times the temperature rise. In practice, kilowatts times 6.8 divided by the rise in degrees Fahrenheit gives gallons per minute. A 6 kW unit at a 35 degree rise gives about 1.2 GPM, and the ThermoMate lists 1.0. An 18 kW unit at a 70 degree rise gives about 1.75 GPM, even though its label says 4.4. Run the numbers for your own house before you buy: subtract your coldest inlet temperature from the temperature you want at the tap, divide 123 by that rise for an 18 kW unit, and the answer is the flow you will really get. If the answer is below what your fixture needs, the heater is the wrong tool for the job.

Size by the coldest water you will see in winter, typically 40 to 45 degrees in cold climates and 60 to 70 in warm ones. A colder inlet means a larger rise for the same target, which means less flow. A unit rated 6.5 GPM at a 45 degree rise delivers about 4.5 at a 77 degree rise. The headline flow assumes the warmest case. A simple way to learn your inlet temperature is to run a cold tap for two minutes in January and measure the water with a kitchen thermometer, which takes no tools and removes the guesswork. Groundwater runs colder in northern states and warmer in the south, and a long buried supply line also changes it.

Current equals power divided by voltage. An 18 kW unit on 240 volts draws about 75 amps, a 6 kW unit about 25 and a 3.5 kW unit on 120 volts about 29. Whole-house electrics often need several breakers and a 200 amp panel. A panel upgrade can cost more than the heater, so price the electrical work first. Houses with 100 amp service are the usual trouble spot, because a single 75 amp appliance leaves almost nothing for the rest of the home. If the quote is more than you wanted to spend, the 6 kW class is the realistic compromise.

An ETL or UL listing means a lab checked the unit against a safety standard, and the ThermoMate 6 kW carries ETL. IPX4 describes splash resistance and is not a listing. Dry-fire cutoff, over-temperature shutoff and ground fault protection all matter. An unlisted heater in a wet location is a risk.

The Rheem 18 kW uses copper immersion elements that are field serviceable, so you can replace a failed element instead of the whole unit. Scale reduces heat transfer and builds faster in hard water. Descale on schedule, and add a filter or softener if your water is very hard. Sealed cheap units are usually replaced after a failure.

Small units serve one sink, and a mid-size 6 kW unit can serve a sink and a laundry tub if they are not used at once. A single low-flow shower in a warm climate can work with 18 kW. Two showers at once need gas or a very large electric system. Match the unit to the number of simultaneous fixtures.

howWeEvaluated.title: Flow arithmetic
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked every flow claim against power and temperature rise. The ThermoMate 6 kW's 1.0 GPM at 35F rise is consistent, while the Rheem 18 kW's 4.4 GPM needs a small rise.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical demand
howWeEvaluated.description: Amperage was compared across the lineup, from about 25 amps on the 6 kW unit to 75 on the 18 kW unit. Heavy loads scored lower for ease of installation.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety listing
howWeEvaluated.description: ETL on the ThermoMate 6 kW and IPX4 on the 4500W unit were weighed. A recognized listing scored higher than a splash rating.

howWeEvaluated.title: Serviceability
howWeEvaluated.description: Field-serviceable elements on the Rheem 18 kW and the scale-resistant design on the ThermoMate units were compared with sealed designs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit at the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Every item is at or under the cap on its live listing. We favored clear data and listings over a bigger kilowatt number.

maintenance.why: Scale cuts heat transfer. Circulate vinegar or descaler through the unit.
Debris restricts flow. Remove the screen and rinse it.
High-current terminals can loosen. Have an electrician check them.
Close the water and confirm the unit cuts power.
Frozen water cracks a heater. Drain it in an unheated space.

faq.q: Can an 18 kW heater run a whole house?
faq.a: Not in cold climates. At a 70 degree rise it delivers about 1.75 GPM, enough for a sink and a low-flow shower only, and not for two showers or a shower plus a dishwasher. A whole house needs 24 kW or more at 240 volts, or a gas unit with a high BTU rating.
It buys point-of-use units up to 18 kW. The cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

faq.q: How big a breaker do I need?
faq.a: Divide watts by volts and add margin. An 18 kW unit needs about 75 amps, while a 6 kW unit needs about 25 amps.
Yes. High-current wiring and permits are standard, and an inspection is often required.

faq.q: Why is my water not hot enough?
faq.a: Flow too high or inlet too cold. Reduce the flow and check the unit's rise.
Five to ten years with descaling. Elements are the wear point, and serviceable ones can be replaced.
